News is always biased based on its source of funding. But they are usually mostly unbiased about things unrelated to their source of funding.

RT has Russian government funding for example, and can be trusted mostly when it comes to things unrelated to the Russian government.

Reuters is owned by https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters a company traded on the stock market. I cant find information definitive but they likely get most revenue via advertising. They can likely be trusted as long as it does not go against world wide advertising interests or major investors in the stock market. Fortunately for Reuters they have a long history and reputation to uphold of being both the first to report on a story and its use of unbiased language in order to deliver news worldwide. For example, Reuters refuses to use the word terrorist among other inherently biased words commenting that "One mans terrorist is another man's freedom fighter"

CNN/FOX/ETC Is funded by almost exclusively the largest American corporations through advertising. These are for a large part the same corporations that buy most controlling influence of the US government. So the US media can be trusted for anything that is not related to USA, its allies or multinational corporations, or almost anything that the western world or multinational corporations have interest in, so the scope of what they can be trusted over is small due to the source of funding.

BBC is funded by mandatory licences what is essentially taxation making it less beholden to major corporations advertising revenue, with a system in place that minimises control by the UK government over content. It may be more trusted related to corporate matters than advert funded news though is still somewhat influenced by the UK government so is better trusted for non UK news and to some extension UKs allies.

In general each news organization can be trusted about most topics except the ones related to their source of funding. As you may have heard, "The customer is always right."
